CLASS 34 · AGES 4–5 · 29 WEATHER LESSONS

Weather, Seasons & What We Wear.

HOW THIS CLASS WORKS

Read the sky, then dress for it.

Every topic in this class has its own step-by-step lesson: look at the picture together, learn what the weather or the garment really is, say the parent script, ask the questions, play the practice game and finish with a small understanding check. The order is gentle: the sun and clouds first, then the weather words, then the day-kinds — sunny, rainy, stormy, snowy, foggy — then the temperatures, the four seasons, and finally the clothes that match every kind of sky.

The best part of this class is that the weather marks your homework. After the sunny-day lesson, a sunny day arrives for free practice; after the raincoat lesson, so does the rain. One topic a day is plenty — the whole class is a month of five-minute sessions, wherever your child’s curiosity points.

WEATHER SAFETY, AGE-HONEST

Small people, real weather.

Weather safety is built into the lessons where it belongs: never staring at the sun, hats and water in the heat, staying inside for storms, penguin steps on ice, bright colours in fog, scarf ends tucked in for climbing. Every rule is phrased for four-year-old bodies and honest about feelings — no scare tactics, no fake promises, just routines that hold.

SEASONS & SPECIAL DAYS

When the season turns, the Hall celebrates.

Weather outside the window is how a child first feels the seasons change — and the seasons bring the special days: October pumpkins, December lights, February hearts. The school’s School Hall keeps the calendar of holidays, the next one always first, with a kid-sized page for each — what it is, why we celebrate, and printable cards to count, name and play.

FROM SKY TIME TO CLOCK TIME

Class 41 · Time & Daily Routine.

Class 34 reads the sky — sun, clouds, rain and the four seasons — and the Time & Daily Routine class reads the clock and the calendar beside it: dawn, noon, dusk and midnight from the card’s four skies, the twelve months the seasons walk through, and the parts of the day your weather clothes change with. Forty-one printable cards for ages 4–5, every one downloadable and printable straight from the class page with its rule and its try-it job right beneath the image.

FROM WEATHER DAYS TO THE WHOLE SKY

Class 43 · Our Earth & Space.

Class 34 dresses for every kind of day — sun hats, raincoats, winter coats — and the Our Earth & Space class explains what the sky is doing up there: twenty-four printable flashcards for ages 4–5 with weather and wind, thunder and lightning, rain and snow, the equator and the poles, and the climate zones that decide what you wear. Every card prints straight from the class page — the weather words your child just used, now with the planets above them.

WEATHER WORKSHEET ACTIVITY · CLASS 34 · AGES 4–5

Animals and Seasons — solve it right on the sheet.

Match animals to their seasons, spot the hibernator, sort the visitors and trace the word ANIMAL.

THE WORKSHEET — WRITE AND DRAW RIGHT ON IT

Your sheet is ready.

Pick a color or the eraser, then match, circle, count, trace and draw straight on the sheet with your finger, a stylus or the mouse. Press Save my work when you are proud — that is what marks this activity cleared for your child.

Solving on the sheet needs JavaScript. The printable twin at /worksheets/weather-seasons-and-what-we-wearanimals-and-seasons/ / always works.

FOR GROWN-UPS

What this worksheet teaches.

What the child is learning: Seasons change what animals do — eating, sleeping, travelling and hiding all follow the weather.

Knowledge to have ready: The four season names, and one familiar animal for each — a spring bird, a summer butterfly, an autumn squirrel, a winter bear.

Why this activity matters: Linking animals to seasons builds the idea that living things respond to the world, not just to us — early science thinking on paper.

  • Season vocabulary
  • Animal names and habitats
  • Sorting and matching
  • Early science reasoning
  • Word tracing

What to say before you start: Every animal has a favourite kind of weather. Let us find out who likes which season.

What to look for on the sheet: Whether your child matches by colour first (easy) or by thinking about the animal first (a real step up).

Questions to ask along the way: Where does the bear go in winter? Which of these animals have you seen for real — and in which season?

Helpful hints without giving it away: Start with the animals your child already knows — the goose and the cat are the easy anchors.

Parent tips: One sheet, one sitting. If the tracing stalls, do the matching first and come back to the word.

Understanding check: Point at the bear: what is it doing this season? A right answer with a reason beats a fast guess.

Real-life practice: On the next walk or park trip, spot one real animal and name its season together.

Autumn and Winter Sorting — solve it right on the sheet.

Match the seasons, circle the right clothes, sort autumn from winter and trace the word AUTUMN.

THE WORKSHEET — WRITE AND DRAW RIGHT ON IT

Your sheet is ready.

Pick a color or the eraser, then match, circle, count, trace and draw straight on the sheet with your finger, a stylus or the mouse. Press Save my work when you are proud — that is what marks this activity cleared for your child.

Solving on the sheet needs JavaScript. The printable twin at /worksheets/weather-seasons-and-what-we-wearautumn-and-winter-sorting/ / always works.

FOR GROWN-UPS

What this worksheet teaches.

What the child is learning: The two cold seasons look and feel different — and they ask for different clothes.

Knowledge to have ready: What autumn looks like (falling leaves, wind) versus winter (snow, bare trees), and which clothes belong to each.

Why this activity matters: Sorting two similar-but-different groups sharpens comparison — the skill underneath all later classification.

  • Comparing two seasons
  • Clothing vocabulary
  • Cutting and sorting
  • Fine motor control
  • Word tracing

What to say before you start: Two chilly seasons, two different looks. Let us sort out which is which.

What to look for on the sheet: Whether the scarf-and-hat items land in winter — that is the subtle pair.

Questions to ask along the way: What do you wear in autumn that you still wear in winter? What changes first?

Helpful hints without giving it away: If sorting stalls, ask "leaves or snow?" — the two pictures sort themselves from that.

Parent tips: Keep the cut pieces in a small bowl so none wander off mid-session.

Understanding check: Ask for one thing that belongs to autumn and one to winter — out loud, no paper.

Real-life practice: On a cool morning, decide together which season it feels like before you dress.

What this worksheet teaches.

Cloud Types — solve it right on the sheet.

Match cumulus, stratus and cirrus to their names, circle the fluffy one, sort the clouds and trace CLOUD.

THE WORKSHEET — WRITE AND DRAW RIGHT ON IT

Your sheet is ready.

Pick a color or the eraser, then match, circle, count, trace and draw straight on the sheet with your finger, a stylus or the mouse. Press Save my work when you are proud — that is what marks this activity cleared for your child.

Solving on the sheet needs JavaScript. The printable twin at /worksheets/weather-seasons-and-what-we-wearcloud-types/ / always works.

FOR GROWN-UPS

What this worksheet teaches.

What the child is learning: Clouds come in kinds — fluffy piles, flat layers, wispy streaks — and each has a name.

Knowledge to have ready: The three cloud names on the sheet (cumulus, stratus, cirrus) and the fluffy-versus-flat contrast.

Why this activity matters: Naming kinds of one thing — clouds — is classification practice with a daily show overhead.

  • Cloud names
  • Observation and comparison
  • Sorting into groups
  • Word tracing
  • Sky vocabulary

What to say before you start: Clouds are not all the same — some sit in piles, some lie flat. Let us learn their names.

What to look for on the sheet: For the wispy streaks — cirrus is the one children most often miss.

Questions to ask along the way: Which cloud is out today? Does it look like the fluffy pile or the flat layers?

Helpful hints without giving it away: Fluffy like a heap of pillows, flat like pancakes — say both while matching.

Parent tips: Keep the sheet on the window ledge for a week and re-check the real sky with it.

Understanding check: Show two clouds from the sheet: which one is stratus? Hands up before answering.

Real-life practice: Watch the sky at breakfast tomorrow and name every cloud you both see.

What this worksheet teaches.

What the child is learning: A grey sky is weather too — cloudy has a name, a look and its own clothes.

Knowledge to have ready: What a cloudy sky looks like next to sunny, rainy and snowy ones, and which clothes fit a grey day.

Why this activity matters: Grey days confuse small children most; naming cloudy gives the day a handle and kills the gloom.

  • Weather recognition
  • Clothing choices
  • Pattern completion
  • Tracing and writing
  • Careful looking

What to say before you start: The sun is hiding today — that has a name too. Let us find the cloudy pictures.

What to look for on the sheet: For the almost-cloudy sky — one small grey cloud counts as cloudy here.

Questions to ask along the way: What does the sky look like right now? What should we wear for it?

Helpful hints without giving it away: Do the circle hunt first, then the words — seeing before naming.

Parent tips: Take the sheet to a window; real sky beats remembered sky at this age.

Understanding check: Ask for one thing cloudy weather is NOT — it proves the sorting stuck.

Real-life practice: Make tomorrow a forecast: tonight your child predicts sunny or cloudy, and morning checks it.

Daylight: Sunrise and Sunset — solve it right on the sheet.

Match the times of day, compare daylight, order the sun arc, trace DAYLIGHT and draw a sunset.

THE WORKSHEET — WRITE AND DRAW RIGHT ON IT

Your sheet is ready.

Pick a color or the eraser, then match, circle, count, trace and draw straight on the sheet with your finger, a stylus or the mouse. Press Save my work when you are proud — that is what marks this activity cleared for your child.

Solving on the sheet needs JavaScript. The printable twin at /worksheets/weather-seasons-and-what-we-weardaylight-sunrise-sunset/ / always works.

FOR GROWN-UPS

What this worksheet teaches.

What the child is learning: The sun makes the day; where it sits in the sky tells you the time.

Knowledge to have ready: Sunrise, noon, sunset and night as positions of the sun — and that summer days are longer.

Why this activity matters: Ordering the day by the sun builds time sense before clocks — the oldest clock there is.

  • Time-of-day vocabulary
  • Sun position and shadow sense
  • Comparing lengths
  • Tracing and writing
  • Drawing what you see

What to say before you start: The sun walks across the sky every day. Let us learn its road.

What to look for on the sheet: For the sun height on the arc — noon sits highest, and that clicks fast once seen.

Questions to ask along the way: Where is the sun when we eat breakfast? Where is it at bedtime in summer?

Helpful hints without giving it away: Act it first: one arm slowly overhead from bed to bed is the whole arc.

Parent tips: This sheet pairs with the rainy-day one — short daylight and long daylight in one week.

Understanding check: Which comes first, sunrise or sunset? Answer without the sheet.

Real-life practice: Catch a real sunset once this week and name what you see with the sheet words.

What this worksheet teaches.

What the child is learning: The year comes in four seasons, each with its own look, weather and clothes.

Knowledge to have ready: The four season names and one clear picture clue for each — blossom, beach, falling leaves, snow.

Why this activity matters: The season cycle is the first big pattern a child meets that repeats every year — naming it orders the whole world.

  • Season names and order
  • Matching pictures to words
  • Clothing sorts
  • Pattern completion
  • Word tracing

What to say before you start: A year has four seasons and each one changes the world outside. Let us match them up.

What to look for on the sheet: For the tree in every picture — same tree, four different dresses.

Questions to ask along the way: Which season is it right now? What will come after it?

Helpful hints without giving it away: The snowman is the fastest anchor — start there and match the rest around it.

Parent tips: Sing the four season names in order before starting; the sheet then checks itself.

Understanding check: Name the four seasons in order, out loud, with fingers counting.

Real-life practice: Start a season wall at home — one drawing per season, added when each arrives.

THE WORKSHEET — WRITE AND DRAW RIGHT ON IT

FOR GROWN-UPS

What this worksheet teaches.

What the child is learning: Ice is water gone cold, and warmth turns it back — melting has an order and a cause.

Knowledge to have ready: The words frost, melt and puddle, and the idea that warmth (sun, hands, warm air) does the melting.

Why this activity matters: Reversible change — freeze it, melt it — is a first science law children can watch in a glass of water.

  • State-of-matter words
  • Ordering a process
  • Predicting outcomes
  • Tracing and writing
  • Observation

What to say before you start: Ice is just water wearing its winter coat. Warmth takes the coat back off.

What to look for on the sheet: For the hair-dryer versus sun comparison — which melts faster and why.

Questions to ask along the way: What made the ice disappear? Where does the puddle come from?

Helpful hints without giving it away: Do the matching with a real ice cube on a saucer beside the sheet.

Parent tips: Freeze a small toy in a cube before the session — the sheet predicts, the cube proves.

Understanding check: Cold makes ice and warmth does what? One word, no paper.

Real-life practice: Leave two ice cubes out — one sunny window, one dark shelf — and race them.

What to say before you start: Some things glow all by themselves and some just catch the light. Let us sort them out.

What this worksheet teaches.

Knowledge to have ready: The four fallers on the sheet and the cold-or-less-cold difference that picks between them.

What this worksheet teaches.

What the child is learning: Weather decides what is safe: kites want calm skies, storms want us inside, sun wants hats.

Knowledge to have ready: The words safe and unsafe, lightning, thunder, rainbow — and hat-sunglasses shade as sun protection.

Why this activity matters: Safety rules stick when a child sorts them on paper first — the sheet does the rehearsing before real wind does.

  • Safety judgement
  • Weather words
  • Matching
  • Tracing and writing
  • Decision making

What to say before you start: Kites love some skies and hate others. Let us learn which is which.

What to look for on the sheet: For the storm-cloud judgement — that is the one real safety decision on the sheet.

Questions to ask along the way: What do we do when thunder starts? Where is the safest place you know?

Helpful hints without giving it away: Safe means calm sky and open space; unsafe means dark clouds or rain.

What to look for on the sheet: For the two rainy squares hiding mid-week; scanning left to right is the real skill here.

Questions to ask along the way: Which weather won the week? Which day would you pick for a picnic?

Helpful hints without giving it away: Point at each day and say its weather out loud before counting anything.

Parent tips: Keep the finished graph on the fridge and start a fresh one next Sunday.

Understanding check: Ask how many rainy days there were — with the sheet turned over.

Real-life practice: Start a real week-chart on the fridge tonight: one sticker or scribble a day.

What to say before you start: Weather readers know tomorrow before it happens — let us read like they do.

What this worksheet teaches.

What the child is learning: Different places can have different weather at the very same moment — a map shows it all at once.

Knowledge to have ready: The four map symbols — sun, rain, snow and wind — and the four town names they match.

Why this activity matters: Reading a map spreads thinking across space instead of one page — geography starts exactly here.

  • Map reading
  • Symbol matching
  • Comparing places

What to say before you start: Four towns, one island, four different skies — let us read them all at once.

What to look for on the sheet: For Snowtown's snowflakes: the coldest answer hides in plain sight, and saying why proves the thinking.

Questions to ask along the way: Which town is ours on this map? What would you pack for Snowtown?

Helpful hints without giving it away: Each town's name is a clue in itself — Rainville is not famous for sunshine.

Parent tips: Draw your own family onto the map — which town would your house be?

Understanding check: Name the weather in two towns, map turned face down.

Real-life practice: Open a real weather map on a phone together and find your own town on it.

What this worksheet teaches.

What the child is learning: Weather has rules that keep us comfortable and safe — dry in rain, warm in cold, water in heat, indoors in a storm.

Knowledge to have ready: The four scenes, the thunder shelter answer, and the three rules: stay dry, stay warm, drink water.

Why this activity matters: Practising safety choices on paper makes the real ones come out automatically — rehearsal without risk.

  • Safety decisions
  • Storm routine
  • Rule matching
  • Word tracing
  • Drawing safety

What to say before you start: Weather is strong, and we are smart — let us learn the moves for every kind of day.

What to look for on the sheet: For the cliff edge — the one unsafe picture, and children spot it with satisfying horror.

Questions to ask along the way: Where do we go when thunder rumbles? What do we drink on a hot day?

Helpful hints without giving it away: Ask of every scene: would a grown-up smile at this? If not — unsafe.

Parent tips: Walk the real storm plan once after the sheet: which room, which seat, which toy.

Understanding check: Two questions, no paper: where in a storm, and what in heat?

Real-life practice: Pack a small weather bag together — hat for sun, umbrella for rain — and keep it by the door.

What this worksheet teaches.

What the child is learning: Weather is measured with real tools — a thermometer for heat, a gauge for rain, a windsock and weathervane for wind.

  • Tool names
  • Matching jobs

What to say before you start: Scientists never guess the weather — they ask their tools. Meet the four of them.

What to look for on the sheet: For the windsock stripes: counting takes patience, and the third sock likes to trick quick eyes.

Questions to ask along the way: Which tool would you want on the balcony? What does our thermometer at home say?

Helpful hints without giving it away: Rain goes in the gauge, wind moves the sock and the vane — the thermometer minds the heat.

Parent tips: A pinwheel or cheap windsock on the balcony makes this sheet come alive all week.

Understanding check: Hold up a finger as a thermometer: what does it measure? Then a finger windsock?

Real-life practice: Build the box invention for real from a cup and a straw, if the design bug bites.

What the child is learning: Wind has a direction, and direction has words — left, right, up and down first, then north, south, east and west.

What to say before you start: Wind never sits still — but it always goes somewhere. Let us name where.

Questions to ask along the way: Which way is the washing-line flag pointing? Where does north sit in our bedroom?

Real-life practice: Watch a real flag or treetop on the walk home and call the direction together.

What the child is learning: Windy is the weather you can hear — and it brings its own things: kites up, hats held, umbrellas tucked.

Knowledge to have ready: Windy next to its three cousins sunny, rainy and cloudy, and the kite as the windy-day star.

  • Weather vocabulary
  • Windy-day choices

  • Word tracing

What to say before you start: You cannot see wind — only what it pushes. Let us spot the pushing day.

What to look for on the sheet: For the umbrella: it opens on rainy days, but wind turns it inside out — that is the thinking test.

Questions to ask along the way: What does wind do to your hair? What flies in wind that will not fly on a still day?

Helpful hints without giving it away: Say each word with its sound — whoosh for wind — and the matching gets easy.

Parent tips: Throw a paper aeroplane on a still day and a windy one, then report back to the sheet.

Understanding check: What comes after the second cloud in the pattern? Answer before pointing.

Real-life practice: On the next windy walk, name three things the wind is moving — bins, leaves, anything.
